newsitem.title: POLAND: Investors worried about Poland's privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Investors worried about Poland's privatisation.

text.p: Foreign investors find Poland increasingly attractive but fear that political disputes may slow down privatisation, members of an international conference said on Thursday.

"Poland has achieved a better balance between monetary, fiscal, legal policies and privatisation than most neighbouring countries," Ivo Stanek, adviser to Bank of Austria's managing board, said during the event, organised by the Economist group.
Poland has attracted nearly $12 billion in foreign direct investment since the 1989 fall of communism and the goverment says the figure should grow to $30 billion by the year 2000.
But some investors were concerned that politcal bickering inside the ruling leftist coalition may slow down the pace of privatisation, especially before parliamentary elections due late next year.
"There was concern that the pace and speed of privatisation might be slowed down by political rivalry," Wiliam Crisp, senior vice-president of the Economist Conferences, told a news conference.

The pace of privatisation divides the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance, a larger and more liberal coalition group, and the Polish Peasant Party, where many politicians say foreign capital inflow is a threat to national interests.
Under a cabinet reshuffle earlier this year, the Peasants took over the treasury ministry, which oversees sales of state assests, and its head Miroslaw Pietrewicz said he would not rush to privatise.

David McQuaid -- one of organisers of the event, attended by more than 100 foreign business executives and Polish cabinet ministers -- said some investors were concerned that inflation might not fall as quickly as the government planned.
He said a continued expansion of credit for consumer goods, which has steeply risen this year, could stir inflation unless the central bank took preventive measures.
The government wants to cut year-on-year inflation to 13 percent in December 1997 from the current 19.5 percent, while maintaining the economic growth at 5.5 percent of gross domestic product.
